segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: See what kind of love the Father has given us: that we should be called children of God—and we are. The reason the world does not know us is that it did not know him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Beloved, we are children of God now, and what we will be has not yet been revealed. We know that when he is revealed we will be like him, because we will see him as he is.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And everyone who has this hope in him purifies themselves, just as he is pure.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Everyone who practices sin also practices lawlessness; sin is lawlessness.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And you know that he was revealed to take away sins, and in him there is no sin.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: No one who remains in him sins; no one who sins has seen him or known him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Little children, let no one deceive you. The one who practices righteousness is righteous, just as he is righteous.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The one who practices sin is from the devil, because the devil has been sinning from the beginning. The Son of God was revealed for this purpose: to undo the works of the devil.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: No one who has been born of God practices sin, because his seed remains in them; and they cannot sin, because they have been born of God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: By this it is clear who are the children of God and who are the children of the devil: everyone who does not practice righteousness is not from God, and neither is the one who does not love their brother or sister.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For this is the message you heard from the beginning: that we should love one another—

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: not like Cain, who was from the evil one and slaughtered his brother. And why did he slaughter him? Because his own works were evil and his brother’s were righteous.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Do not be surprised, brothers and sisters, if the world hates you.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: We know that we have crossed over from death into life, because we love our brothers and sisters. The one who does not love remains in death.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Everyone who hates their brother or sister is a murderer, and you know that no murderer has eternal life remaining in them.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: By this we have come to know love: he laid down his life for us. And we ought to lay down our lives for our brothers and sisters.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But whoever has the world’s goods and sees their brother or sister in need, yet shuts off compassion from them—how does the love of God remain in such a person?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Little children, let us not love with word or with tongue, but in deed and in truth.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: By this we will know that we are from the truth, and before him we will reassure our hearts

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: whenever our hearts condemn us; for God is greater than our hearts, and he knows everything.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Beloved, if our hearts do not condemn us, we have confidence before God,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and whatever we ask we receive from him, because we keep his commandments and do what is pleasing in his sight.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And this is his commandment: that we believe in the name of his Son Jesus Christ and love one another, just as he commanded us.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Whoever keeps his commandments remains in him, and he in them. And by this we know that he remains in us: by the Spirit he has given us.

notes.note: These words are present in the earliest manuscripts but missing from most later ones, which is why the King James Version does not have them. They are generally accepted as original.

The Greek verb has no stated subject, so the clause can also be read “when it is revealed,” meaning what we will be. “He” is chosen because the same phrase in 2:28 refers to Christ’s coming and the next words speak of seeing him. Both readings have scholarly support.

Here and in verses 5, 7 and 16 the Greek uses an emphatic pronoun, literally “that one.” In this letter it regularly points to Jesus. The plain “him” elsewhere in the chapter is often ambiguous between God and Christ, and the translation leaves that ambiguity in place.

The Greek verb is the ordinary word for staying or continuing somewhere. “Abide” is traditional in John’s writings but is no longer everyday English. “Remain” is used throughout the chapter so that the repetition stays visible.

notes.phrase: No one who remains in him sins
notes.note: The Greek present tense can describe a continuing pattern, so many versions render “keeps on sinning” here and in verse 9, which eases the tension with 1:8–2:1, where the author says that claiming to be without sin is self-deception. Whether the tense alone carries that weight is disputed. The translation leaves the statement as stark as the Greek and does not resolve the question.

The verb’s basic use is loosening or untying, and by extension dismantling, annulling or bringing something to an end. “Destroy” is the usual rendering and is not wrong. “Undo” keeps the sense of reversing what the devil has done.

The image is most often taken as God’s own life-giving principle, variously identified as his word, his Spirit or the new nature, implanted in the believer as a father’s seed begets a child. Because the word can also mean “offspring,” a minority reads “God’s offspring remain in him,” that is, in God. The translation follows the majority reading.

The Greek word, literally “brother,” was the ordinary term for a fellow member of the community regardless of sex, and its plural regularly included women. It is rendered “brother or sister” and “brothers and sisters” where a fellow believer is meant, and “brother” for Cain’s actual brother in verse 12. Several modern versions do the same.

The verb is stronger than the usual words for killing. It was used for slaughtering animals, especially in sacrifice, and for butchering people violently. Elsewhere in the New Testament it occurs only in Revelation. Most modern versions soften it to “murdered,” which also blurs the distinction from the different word for “murderer” in verse 15.

notes.traditional: shall assure our hearts before him. For if our heart condemn us, God is greater than our heart
notes.note: The grammar of verses 19–20 is among the most difficult in the letter. The verb can mean “persuade” or “set at rest,” and the connecting word that opens verse 20 can be read as “that,” “because” or “whenever.” The rendering follows the common view that God’s greater knowledge is a comfort to a self-accusing conscience. Some have instead taken it as a warning that God judges more strictly than the heart does.

The word originally meant freedom to speak one’s mind, and by this period it also meant the assurance of someone who can stand before a superior without fear or shame. “Confidence” conveys this better than “boldness,” which can suggest audacity. Most modern versions make the same choice here, and the difference is one of English nuance more than of meaning.
